attribution.note: Marcus's own words on his own Substack, written in the first person.

semantics.note: The revision keeps 'seem to me', 'still' and 'merely hint'. It is a subjective, evaluative observation with no standard for adequacy or understanding.

contract.note: The contract rightly says the full statement is a personal impression with no definite support or contradiction condition. Scoring it would mean the evaluator inventing tests.

evidence.note: Ars Technica, April 2024, reports Grok making up headlines. It concerns only Grok and only fabrication. It cannot settle adequacy or understanding for both chatbots.

reviews.rationale: The statement is framed as Marcus's impression ('seem to me') and uses evaluative terms (wildly inadequate, precious little understanding) that have no operational standard. Documented Grok fabrications touch only the narrow hallucination point, not the whole judgement, so the claim cannot be scored.

attribution.note: Marcus's own words in his post.

semantics.note: A faithful summary of a firm observation about Grok's temporal reasoning at the time of the post.

contract.note: The plain reading (unreliable on elementary dates and chronology) is ordinary and fair. A May 2024 window is a reasonable inference from 'yesterday'.

evidence.note: xAI's own Grok-1.5 announcement from March 2024. It is a company disclosure dated before the window, with no temporal-reasoning test, so it is background only.

reviews.rationale: The packet has no independent test or authenticated transcript of Grok's temporal reasoning in May 2024. The only item is a company announcement that does not address the claim, and Marcus's own example cannot prove itself.

attribution.note: Marcus's own words in his post, describing his testing of Grok.

semantics.note: It captures the three parts: frequent errors, inconsistent answers and overconfidence. The 'sometimes right' allowance is implied but not stated.

contract.note: The plain reading is fair: recurring errors, real inconsistency and overconfidence, with 'never in doubt' read as rhetoric, not literally.

evidence.note: Tom's Guide, May 8, 2024: a firsthand review saying Grok hallucinates and gets information wrong. This supports only the existence of errors. It gives no rate, no repeated-prompt test and no measure of confidence.

reviews.rationale: The one item in the window shows Grok made some errors, which fits 'sometimes right' as well as 'frequently wrong'. Nothing measures how often it erred, how its answers varied on the same question, or how confident it was. Not enough to settle the claim.

attribution.note: Marcus's own words in his post.

semantics.note: Reading 'Musk' as xAI and keeping Meta's 'mostly' is faithful. 'Bigger and bigger' is shortened to 'bigger', with little loss.

contract.note: The plain reading is broadly fair. It rightly flags that the result depends on how 'just' and 'mostly' are read, and it does not treat one alternative Meta program as disproof.

evidence.note: Meta's own Llama 3 post, April 2024, reports a much larger training set. A company disclosure, but it supports only the Meta scaling part, not that scaling dominated.
Meta's own V-JEPA post, February 2024, shows a non-LLM research line. Its relative size is unknown, so it does not contradict 'mostly'.
xAI's own Grok-1.5V post, April 2024, announces a multimodal model. It does not show a departure from scaling LLMs or any increase in scale.

reviews.rationale: The evidence shows Meta scaled Llama 3 and also ran V-JEPA. It does not show what share of Meta's effort went to scaling. For xAI it shows neither successive increases in scale nor a real alternative approach. Both parts remain unsettled.
